title: Make WebGL context loss and restore return product readiness to a known state

scope.subject: Reuse the existing R3F WebGLRenderer and web-platform context-loss lifecycle so transient context loss invalidates world readiness immediately and restoration must reacquire render readiness without creating another renderer or recovery manager

research_summary: The product already has one React Three Fiber Canvas, Three.js context restoration support, a terminal pagehide release path, and world readiness signals. The missing behavior is state correctness during a recoverable WebGL loss: readiness can remain semantically stale while the underlying context is unavailable. Reuse the existing canvas WebGL context events to mark the renderer lost/active, invalidate product world readiness on loss, and let the existing CinematicPipeline reacquire readiness from real post-restore frames. No new renderer, retry loop, GPU registry, or recovery scheduler is required.

sources.finding: React Three Fiber Canvas owns the existing Three.js WebGLRenderer and its normal renderer lifecycle, so recovery should stay attached to that single renderer rather than construct a replacement.
Three.js WebGLRenderer owns the current WebGL context and handles browser context restoration internally; product code can preserve renderer ownership while invalidating higher-level readiness.

The canvas webglcontextlost event is the platform signal that rendering resources are unavailable; cancelling a synthetic loss permits later restoration and gives the product a concrete invalidation boundary.
The webglcontextrestored event marks restoration of the context, after which resources/render state must be re-established before application-level readiness is trusted again.

search_ladder.conclusion: This is a bounded recovery-state correction inside the already selected renderer stack, not a replacement rendering application.
Keep the single R3F-owned Three.js renderer and its built-in context restoration lifecycle as the renderer authority.
Three.js and the browser context lifecycle already expose the required recovery boundary, so a separate GPU recovery subsystem would duplicate ownership.
Use the standard canvas WebGL context loss/restoration events as the precise trigger for invalidating and reacquiring product readiness.

candidates.name: Existing R3F/Three renderer context restoration lifecycle
candidates.source: Current single R3F Canvas and Three.js WebGLRenderer
candidates.reason: It preserves the existing renderer/camera authority and already handles the low-level WebGL restoration mechanics needed by the product.

candidates.name: Standard WebGL context lost/restored events
candidates.source: Browser WebGL context lifecycle events used through the existing canvas
candidates.reason: These events provide the exact loss/restore boundary without polling, timers, replacement contexts, or a second lifecycle owner.

decision.rationale: Keep R3F/Three as the sole renderer authority and reuse standard WebGL context events only as readiness invalidation boundaries. On loss, clear stale world paint/pipeline/screenshot readiness immediately; on restore, retain the same renderer and require the existing pipeline to earn readiness again from real rendered frames. This is lower cost and more correct than adding a recovery manager or recreating the Canvas.
decision.fallback: If a specific upstream pass cannot survive Three.js context restoration, isolate and recreate only that pass after measured evidence; do not replace the Canvas or introduce a second renderer.
